info.description: The curriculum introduces students to topics in computer architecture that are considered fundamental to an understanding of the digital systems underpinnings of computer systems.

info.courseDetails:
This is a 4 credit course with emphasis on applied programming skills; please take it into consideration when planning your other courses. 

Visit previous offering page, section Check Yourself: https://www.cs.sfu.ca/~ashriram/Courses/CS295//labs.html#labs. 2. Be completely comfortable running, the program noted within the link. 3. Run it in CSIL and remotely to CSIL. Please contact asadvise@sfu.ca with any questions." 
 
Overview: This course should develop students' sense of what really happens when software runs — and that this question can be answered at several levels of abstraction, including the hardware architecture level, the assembly level and the C programming level. The core around which the course is built is C, assembly, and low-level data representation, but this is connected to higher levels (roughly how basic other programming langauges could could be implemented), lower levels (the general structure of a processor), and the role of the processor and its how it is implemented. This course provides an introduction to computer organization, systems programming and the hardware/software interface. Topics include instruction sets, computer arithmetic, datapath design, data formats, addressing modes, memory hierarchies including caches and virtual memory, and multicore architectures. Students learn assembly language programming and design a pipelined RISC V processor. The course is open to any undergraduate who has mastered the 125/135 material.

RISC V: This version of the course will study the core components in computer organization through the lens of the RISC-V (V : Five) ISA. RISC V is a modern open source instruction set that enables students to learn both assembly-level programming and the digital design of a processor. **This course is a hands-on, programming-heavy course**. We will discuss the fundamental design and engineering trade-offs in computer organization at every level. 

Course Offer Plan 4 Credits:
- Lab: There will be dedicated lab days. (required lab). Attendance is required and counts towards your overall grade. In-person. **Midterms and Exams will be held during the lab so carefully select your lab slot.**
- Quizzes - A quiz every 1-2 weeks, administered and graded online.  
- Midterms and Exams: 2 Midterms and 1 Final.

Textbooks

Please try and obtain the e-versions of these text books. Please continue to check our course outline for further information. 

Workload comments
This is a 4 credit course.
 The comments below are provided based on past student experience. It is to enable you to appropriately select the term in which you take 295. As the first introduction to systems, 295 is an intense course and requires 1) Attending 3hrs of lectures  2) 20m of quizes/week 3) 1 hr of labs/week 4) 5 hrs / week for take-home programming assignments (assumes familiarity with C/C++). Your learning outcomes in 295 are highly dependent on whether you are comfortable with the material, and C/C++ programming from 125 and 135. 295 is set up to make you a better programmer and this requires the student to invest the requisite time. As our grading distribution shows; all components are equally important. Hence, please take it in the term that you can dedicate the time.

Topics

  • RISC-V
  • Bits, Arrays, Pointers
  • Number formats 
  • Memory layout
  • Caches
  • Vectorization
  • Digital logic: Combinational and Sequential
  • Processor Pipeline
  • Parallelism
  • Logical and arithmetic operations
